All of this money comes from her job at a local movie theatre, so I can't exactly cut her off. I can't explain why, but something about it drives me up the \*\*\*\*ing wall. Maybe it's because Toni Collette was so creepy? Maybe I just want to spend some quality time with my daughter instead of watching her waste her life in her bedroom. I hear my sister talk about dropping her daughter off at soccer, or how her son's the lead in the school play, and then think about how my daughter's upstairs building a tiny cottage with tweezers. She hasn't ever really shown interest in any hobbies before, so I thought it would be grateful that she's finally good at something, but mostly I'm just annoyed. I try to ask her if she'd like to go for a walk with me, or sign up for cheerleading, but she always says no. My husband thinks its sweet and has started letting her put them around the house and in his office at work. prediction.raw: 1 (You would be the asshole). As a parent, it's natural to have concerns about your child's hobbies and how they might impact their future. However, in this scenario, your daughter is 17, has a job, and is using her own money to fund her hobby. She's also maintaining good grades and completing her chores, which suggests that her hobby isn't negatively impacting her responsibilities. It's also important to consider that having a unique hobby like building miniatures can be a great way for your daughter to express her creativity and develop skills like attention to detail, patience, and problem-solving. These skills can be valuable in many areas of life, even if they might not be directly applicable to a specific job. Rather than trying to dictate what hobby your daughter should pursue, it might be more productive to try to understand why you're feeling annoyed by her hobby. Is it because you feel like you're not spending enough quality time with her? Are you worried that her hobby is somehow "unconventional" or won't lead to traditional success? It might be helpful to have an open and honest conversation with your daughter about your concerns, but also to listen to her perspective and try to understand what she enjoys about building miniatures. You could also try to find ways to engage with her hobby, even if it's not something you're personally interested in. For example, you could ask her to show you her latest project or offer to help her find new materials or techniques to try. Ultimately, it's your daughter's life and her decision what hobbies she wants to pursue. As her parent, your role is to support and guide her, not to dictate what she should or shouldn't be doing.
